title: Valid Number
description: Brute force to optimized: splitting into mantissa and exponent substrings to validate separately versus a single pass over the string tracking a small set of state flags.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s, return true if s is a valid number, and false otherwise. A valid number follows an optional sign, a decimal part (digits, digits followed by a dot, digits with a dot and more digits, or a dot followed by digits), and an optional exponent part (an "e" or "E", an optional sign, and required digits).

blocks.text: Given s, decide whether it matches the shape of a valid number: an optional leading sign, then a decimal portion (which must contain at least one digit, with at most one dot), optionally followed by an exponent marker (e or E), an optional sign, and at least one digit.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking a Form Field Against a Strict Format
blocks.text: Picture validating a numeric input field: a sign is allowed only at the very start (or right after "e"), a decimal point can appear at most once, and if an exponent marker appears, it absolutely must be followed by at least one digit, an "e" with nothing after it is not acceptable.

blocks.caption: The valid number shape: optional sign, decimal part, optional exponent part

blocks.text: Each of these follows the grammar: a sign only at valid positions, at most one dot, and any exponent marker followed by at least one digit.

"1e" fails because the exponent has no digits after it; "99e2.5" fails because a dot cannot appear in the exponent part; "--6" and "-+3" fail because a sign can only appear at the very start or immediately after "e".

Before trying to match everything in one pass, notice the string cleanly splits into two independent pieces: the part before "e" (the decimal mantissa) and the part after it (the integer exponent), if an "e" is present at all.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A valid number always has, at most, one "e" or "E", splitting it into a mantissa and an exponent, each with its own simpler grammar.

Observation 2: The exponent part, if present, must be a plain optionally-signed integer, no dot allowed.

Observation 3: The mantissa part must be a plain optionally-signed decimal, at most one dot, and at least one digit somewhere in it.

Observation 4: Once these two smaller, well-defined checks exist, splitting on "e" and applying one check to each half solves the whole problem.

This leads to two valid strategies: split on "e" and validate the two halves with focused helper checks, or scan the whole string once, tracking a small set of flags (seen a digit, seen a dot, seen an exponent) and rejecting immediately the moment a rule is broken.
Split the string on "e" or "E" if present, validate the part before it as a decimal number, and validate the part after it as a plain integer.

items: Look for "e" or "E" in the string.
If found, split into a mantissa (before) and an exponent (after); the exponent must be a non-empty, optionally-signed run of digits.
If not found, the entire string is the mantissa.
The mantissa must be a non-empty, optionally-signed run of digits, optionally containing a single dot, with at least one digit somewhere in it.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: split into mantissa and exponent, validate each independently

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Splitting on "e" first isolates two genuinely independent sub-grammars, each far simpler to validate on its own.
is_valid_integer and is_valid_decimal are small, focused helpers, each responsible for exactly one part of the overall shape.
Multiple string operations, find, split, substring, are used freely for clarity, at the cost of a few extra passes over short substrings.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), where n is the length of s, though several string operations (find, split, substring) each scan their own portion.
Space: O(n) for the substrings created during splitting.

Limitation: creating separate substrings for the mantissa and exponent, and further splitting the mantissa on a dot, does more allocation and re-scanning than strictly necessary, a single combined pass can validate everything with fixed extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why splitting into substrings is more work than needed: every rule (sign placement, at most one dot, exponent needs digits) can be checked while scanning the original string once, without ever materializing a smaller copy of it.

What state needs to be tracked while scanning: whether a digit has been seen at all, whether a dot has been seen, whether an exponent marker has been seen, and whether a digit has been seen since the last exponent marker.

How does each character update that state: a digit sets "seen a digit" (and "seen a digit after exponent" if an exponent has appeared); a sign is only valid at position 0 or immediately after an exponent marker; a dot is only valid if no dot and no exponent has been seen yet; an exponent marker is only valid if one has not already appeared and at least one digit has been seen before it.

The core idea: walk the string once, carrying a handful of boolean flags, and reject immediately the moment any character breaks a rule, accepting only if a digit was seen overall and, if an exponent appeared, a digit was seen after it too.

Scan the string left to right exactly once, maintaining flags for whether a digit, a dot, and an exponent marker have been seen so far, and whether a digit has appeared since the most recent exponent marker. Reject immediately on any character that violates the rules for its position, and accept only if a digit was seen overall and, if an exponent appeared, a digit followed it.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one pass, a handful of flags, reject the instant a rule breaks

blocks.text: Each flag captures exactly the one piece of history needed to validate the next character: whether any digit has appeared at all, whether a dot has already been used, whether an exponent marker has already been used, and whether a digit has appeared since the most recent exponent marker. Checking a character against these flags, in order, enforces every rule of the grammar without ever needing to look backward or split the string into pieces.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass over the string.
Space: O(1), just a handful of boolean flags.

blocks.text: Valid Number is fundamentally a grammar-checking problem: the key to a clean solution is identifying the small set of state (has a digit, dot, or exponent been seen, and has a digit followed the exponent) that fully determines whether each new character is acceptable.

items: Allowing a sign to appear anywhere, instead of only at the very start or immediately after an exponent marker.
Forgetting that an exponent marker must be followed by at least one digit, "1e" alone is not valid.
Allowing a dot to appear after an exponent marker, or more than once anywhere.

blocks.text: Walking through the full grammar out loud first, sign placement, dot rules, and exponent rules, before writing any code, is the best way to avoid missing one of this problem's many small edge cases.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid splitting the string", think: a single pass with a handful of boolean flags capturing exactly what has been seen so far.
If the interviewer says "what breaks your solution", think: signs in the wrong position, more than one dot, or an exponent marker with no digit before or after it.

items: How would you extend this grammar to also accept a leading or trailing whitespace, as some numeric parsers do?
Could this validation be expressed as a small deterministic finite automaton, and what would its states be?
How would you adapt this to also parse out the numeric value, not just validate the format?
Any string-validation problem with a strict grammar, best solved with a small set of tracked flags in a single pass rather than a fragile all-in-one regular expression.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches run in O(n) time. The brute force uses O(n) space for the split substrings; the single-pass state-flag version uses O(1) space.

items: Pattern: grammar validation using a small set of state flags tracked across a single pass.

Core Idea: track whether a digit, a dot, and an exponent marker have been seen, plus whether a digit has followed the most recent exponent marker, and reject the instant any character violates the rules implied by that state.
Time: O(n) for both approaches.
Space: O(n) for the brute force's split substrings, O(1) for the single-pass version.
Most Important Observation: a handful of boolean flags fully capture everything needed to validate the next character, no backward look or string splitting required.
Interview Difficulty: the individual rules are simple, but there are many of them, correctness depends on not missing one.
One line memory trick: one pass, four flags, sign only at the start or right after e.
